newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans to end monopoly on sugar exports.
newsitem.headline: India plans to end monopoly on sugar exports.

text.p: The Indian government has decided to authorise more firms to export sugar, ending a trading agency's monopoly over foreign sales, a government official said on Friday.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said Prime Minister H. D. Deve Gowda's cabinet took the decision on Wednesday to end the monopoly of the Indian Sugar and General Industries Export Import Corp (ISIGEC).

"Since there is surplus production, ISIGEC, State Trading Corporation and individuals and firms registered with APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority), would also be authorised to export sugar," the official said.
The official confirmed reports in the Business Standard and Business Line newspapers published on Friday.
The Business Standard said a formal announcement of the decision was put off to allow the government to gauge its political implications.
ISIGEC is a private company set up by the sugar milling industry. Currently all exports are funnelled, or "canalised", through ISIGEC.
Currently the Sugar Export Promotion Act (SEPA) of 1958 stipulates that the country can export up to 20 percent of total sugar production.
The official said SEPA would have to be amended before allowing new players to export.
"The act will be amended as soon as possible," he said.

On Monday, Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah told parliament the government had authorised the Food Ministry to permit the export of 1.0 million tonnes of sugar in the 1996/97 (October-September) season.
It was not clear whether SEPA would be amended to allow more than 20 percent of total production to be exported.
"We have a surfeit of production," the official said.
The industry expects sugar output in 1995/96 to touch 16.45 million tonnes, up sharply from 14.6 million in the previous season.
